'''Moritz Werner Fenchel''' ({{IPA|de|ˈfɛnçəl|lang}}; 3 May 1905&nbsp;–&nbsp;24 January 1988) was a German-Danish [[mathematician]] known for his contributions to [[geometry]] and to [[Optimization (mathematics)|optimization theory]].  Fenchel established the basic results of [[convex analysis]] and nonlinear optimization theory which would, in time, serve as the foundation for [[nonlinear programming]].  A German-born Jew and early refugee from Nazi suppression of intellectuals, Fenchel lived most of his life in Denmark.  Fenchel's monographs and lecture notes are considered influential.

==Biography==

===Early life and education===
Fenchel was born on 3 May 1905 in [[Berlin]], Germany,<ref name=Theseus>{{cite web|title=Theseus Curriculum Vitae of Werner Fenchel|url=http://www.math.ku.dk/ths/fenchel_w/|work=Theseus|access-date=28 December 2012|archive-date=7 February 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120207012518/http://www.math.ku.dk/ths/fenchel_w/|url-status=dead}}</ref> his younger brother was the Israeli film director and architect [[Heinz Fenchel]].

Fenchel studied mathematics and physics at the [[University of Berlin]] between 1923 and 1928.<ref name="Theseus" />  He wrote his doctorate thesis in [[geometry]] (''Über Krümmung und Windung geschlossener Raumkurven'')<ref>{{cite web|title=Virtual Internet Authority File 2603673|url=http://viaf.org/viaf/2603673/|access-date=28 December 2012}}</ref> under [[Ludwig Bieberbach]].<ref name="Theseus" />

===Professorship in Germany===
From 1928 to 1933, Fenchel was Professor [[E. Landau]]'s Assistant at the [[University of Göttingen]].  During a one-year leave (on [[Rockefeller Fellowship]]) between 1930 and 1931, Fenchel spent time in Rome with [[Tullio Levi-Civita]], as well as in [[Copenhagen]] with [[Harald Bohr]] and [[Tommy Bonnesen]].
He visited Denmark again in 1932.<ref name="Theseus" />

===Professorship in exile===
Fenchel taught at Göttingen until 1933, when the [[Law for the Restoration of the Professional Civil Service|Nazi discrimination laws]] led to [[Racial policy of Nazi Germany|mass-firings of Jews]].<ref>{{cite journal|last=Kiselman|first=Christer|title=Werner Fenchel: A pioneer in convexity theory|pages=133–152|year=2019|journal=Göteborg: Nationellt centrum för matematikutbildning|volume=61|issue=2–4|url=http://www.cb.uu.se/~kiselman/fenchel.pdf|quote=Many scientists in Germany lost their jobs after the ''Nazi Machtübernahme'' in 1933. Fenchel was one of them. It seems appropriate to describe in some detail this development, which is of interest also because of the general decline of science and culture in Germany. See also Gordin (2015: Chapter 7, Unspeakable)|archive-date=2 July 2018|access-date=8 July 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180702011115/http://www.cb.uu.se/~kiselman/fenchel.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Fenchel emigrated to Denmark somewhere between April and September 1933, ultimately obtaining a position at the [[University of Copenhagen]].  In December 1933, Fenchel married fellow German refugee mathematician [[Käte Sperling]].<ref name="Theseus" />

When [[Occupation of Denmark|Germany occupied Denmark]], Fenchel and roughly eight-thousand other Danish Jews [[Rescue of the Danish Jews|received refuge]] in Sweden, where he taught (between 1943 and 1945) at the Danish School in [[Lund]].<ref name="Theseus" /> After the Allied powers' [[Occupation of Denmark#Hardship and the end of the war|liberation of Denmark]], Fenchel returned to Copenhagen.

===Professorship postwar===
In 1946, Fenchel was elected a member of the [[Royal Danish Academy of Sciences and Letters]].<ref name="Theseus" />

On leave between 1949 and 1951, Fenchel taught in the U.S. at the [[University of Southern California]], [[Stanford University]], and [[Princeton University]].<ref name="Theseus" />

From 1952 to 1956 Fenchel was the professor in mechanics at the Polytechnic in Copenhagen.<ref name="Theseus" />

From 1956 to 1974 he was the professor in mathematics at the [[University of Copenhagen]].<ref name="Theseus" />

===Last years, death, legacy===
Professor Fenchel died on 24 January 1988.<ref name="Theseus" />

==Geometric contributions==

===Convex geometry===
{{main|Convex geometry}}
{{see also|Alexandrov–Fenchel inequality}}

===Optimization theory===
{{main|Convex analysis}}
{{see also|Convex set|Convex cone|Convex function}}
{{see also|Legendre-Fenchel transformation|Fenchel's duality theorem}}
Fenchel lectured on "Convex Sets, Cones, and Functions" at Princeton University in the early 1950s. His lecture notes shaped the field of [[convex analysis]], according to the monograph ''Convex Analysis'' of [[R. T. Rockafellar]].
